opus-5.5.text:
I think the key word is really "memory," and maybe also "proactiveness." Today, when you use most agents, every session starts almost from zero. You tell it what you want, it does the task, and then it forgets you. That's more like hiring a very capable stranger every time than having an assistant who actually knows you.

A truly personalized agent should accumulate an understanding of you over time: your habits, your preferences, the way you like things done, even the things you never explicitly say. A good human assistant learns that you prefer short emails, or that you never take meetings before ten, without you writing a rule for it. They pick it up from interaction. I think agents need the same ability to learn continually from their experience with a specific person, not just from a giant pretraining corpus.

From a technical point of view, I see this as a reinforcement learning problem. Each user is like a different environment with a different reward function, and that reward is mostly implicit. You don't give the agent a score. You accept its suggestion, or you edit it, or you ignore it. So the agent has to infer what you want from those weak signals and keep adapting. Right now we're good at training one big model offline with a fixed objective. We're much less good at letting a model keep improving online, for one person, safely and efficiently.

The second part is proactiveness. Today's agents mostly wait for your instruction. But if an agent really understands you, it should sometimes act before you ask: notice that something needs attention, prepare things in advance, ask the right clarifying question at the right moment. That's hard because being proactive in the wrong way is really annoying. It has to have good judgment about when to step in and when to stay quiet, and that judgment is itself very personal.

So the agent I imagine is less like a tool you operate and more like a partner that grows with you. The longer you use it, the more it becomes *your* agent, different from anyone else's. I don't think we're there yet, but I think that's where the field is heading, and RL is going to be a central piece of getting there.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent should learn a user's habits and preferences over time, but it does not mention learning which service platform the user chooses or using that preference for future transactions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because "personalized" gets thrown around but people usually mean something pretty shallow by it—like the model remembers your name, or you can set a system prompt that says "be concise." That's customization. It's not really personalization.

What I actually envision is something closer to how a good collaborator who's worked with you for years behaves. They don't just know facts about you, they've built a model of how you think. They know that when you say "just make it work," you mean a quick hack is fine, but when you say "let's do this properly," you want the full thing. They know which of your decisions you'll regret and gently push back on those. They know when to interrupt you and when to leave you alone.

And the key thing is, none of that is written down anywhere. It's learned through interaction. So to me the real question is: how does an agent learn from the trajectory of working with one specific person, not from the whole internet?

I think this has to come from the agent's own experience. You can't pretrain it in. Each person's preferences are a kind of hidden state, and the agent has to infer it by acting, observing your reactions, and updating. That's basically a reinforcement learning problem, honestly—a very long-horizon one, where the reward signal is noisy and sparse. You might only find out a month later that the way you organized someone's codebase annoyed them.

There are a couple of hard pieces. One is memory—not retrieval of chat logs, but actually compressing a year of interactions into something that changes behavior. Another is that the agent needs to be a bit exploratory. If it only ever does what it thinks you want, it never learns what you'd actually prefer. A good human assistant occasionally tries something slightly different and watches your face. We need agents that do that, carefully.

And then there's the question of what's shared versus what's yours. I don't think every user should have their own fully fine-tuned model—that's expensive and kind of unnecessary. The base capabilities are shared. But the layer on top, the model of you, that should be yours, and ideally it should be portable. If I switch tools, the thing that knows me should come with me.

So, less "AI that you configure," more "AI that grows up with you." That's the version I find exciting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning a person’s preferences through interaction, but does not mention learning their preferred service platform or using it for future transactions.

astra-6.text:
I envision a personalized AI agent as something that gradually learns how to work with you. It understands your goals, your preferences, and the context behind what you’re asking—not just the words in a single prompt.

For example, when you ask it to help plan your day, it should understand which commitments matter most to you, when you prefer to focus, and where you want flexibility. But it should also recognize that your preferences can change. Personalization shouldn’t mean putting you into a fixed category.

The key is giving you control over that relationship: what it remembers, what it can act on, and when it needs to ask. Over time, it could take more initiative as you develop trust. To me, a good personalized agent helps you spend less effort explaining yourself while still making it easy to correct its assumptions.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning a user’s goals and preferences generally, but does not mention learning their habitual service platform choice or using it for future transactions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a more personalized AI agent should understand not just what you ask, but what you’re trying to achieve. Two people can ask the same question and need very different kinds of help, depending on their background, their preferences, and the situation.

That understanding should develop through working together. The agent learns how you like to communicate, remembers the context you choose to share, and adapts when your priorities change. Over time, you spend less effort explaining yourself and more time doing what matters to you.

But personalization also needs to be under your control. You should be able to see what the agent remembers, correct it, and tell it to forget something. And it should know when to act independently and when to ask. For me, the goal is an agent that becomes a better collaborator over time—one that understands you while still helping you consider new perspectives.
